text:
I once did you a wrong, Johannes; I wanted to make amends for it, put it right. I really have a surprise that I think ... that is to say, that I hope you will be pleased by. I cannot say any more. But this time I will ask you to be present.

If it can give you any pleasure, then I shall come.

Will you?

Yes, I thank you for your kindness.

When he had gone down into the forest, he turned around and looked back. She had seated herself; the basket stood beside her. He did not go home, but continued wandering along the road and back again. A thousand thoughts struggled within him. A surprise? She had said it just now, only a moment ago; her voice had trembled. A hot and nervous joy arose within him, made his heart pound violently, and he felt himself lifted from the road on which he walked. And was it merely chance that she was dressed in yellow today as well? He had looked at her hand where the ring had once been—she wore no ring.

An hour passed. The vapors of the forest and the fields surrounded him, entered into his breath, into his heart. He sat down, lay back with his hands clasped beneath his neck, and listened for a time to the cuckoo’s piping on the other side of the inlet. Passionate birdsong quivered in the air around him.

So he had experienced it again! When she came up to him in the quarry in her yellow dress and with her blood-red hat, she looked like a wandering butterfly stepping from stone to stone and stopping before him. I did not want to disturb you, she had said, smiling; her smile was red, her whole face lit up, she scattered stars. Some fine blue veins had appeared on her neck, and the few freckles beneath her eyes gave her a warm color. She was in her twentieth summer.

A surprise? What was her intention? Did she perhaps mean to show him his books, to lay out those two or three volumes and please him by telling him that she had bought them all and cut open their pages? There you are, one tiny little token of attention and gentle consolation! Do not disdain my modest contribution!

He rose abruptly and remained standing. Victoria came back; her basket was empty.

You found no flowers? he asked absently.

No, I gave it up. Nor did I look; I merely sat there.

He said:

While I remember it: you must not go about thinking that you have done me any wrong. You have nothing to make amends for with any kind of gentle consolation.

No? she answered, taken aback. She thought further about it, looked at him, and pondered. No? I thought that at the time
«+++ I did not want you to go on bearing a grudge against me all the time for what happened.

No, I bear you no grudge.

She thought for another moment. Suddenly she drew herself up.

Then that is well, she said. No, I ought to have known that. It did not leave so great an impression. Well, well, then we shall speak no more of it.

No, let us not. My impressions are as immaterial to you now as they were before.

Goodbye, she said. Goodbye for now.

Goodbye, he answered. |

They went their separate ways. He stopped and turned around. There she went now. He stretched out his hands and whispered, speaking tender words to himself: I bear you no grudge, no, no, I do not; I still love you, love you ....

Victoria! he called.

She heard it, started, and turned around, but continued walking.

Several days passed. Johannes went about in the greatest agitation and did not work, did not sleep; he spent almost the whole day in the forest. He climbed onto the great mound of pinewood where the Castle’s flagpole stood; there was a flag on the pole. A flag had also been raised on the Castle’s round tower.

A strange excitement seized him. Guests were to come to the Castle; there was to be a celebration.

The afternoon was still and warm; the river ran like a pulse through the hot landscape. A steamship glided in toward land and left a fan of white streaks spreading across the inlet. Now four carriages drove out from the Castle courtyard and took the road down to the landing.

The ship docked; gentlemen and ladies came ashore and took their places in the carriages. Then a succession of shots began to crack from the Castle; two men stood atop the round tower and loaded and fired, loaded and fired hunting guns. When they had discharged twenty-one shots, the carriages rolled in through the Castle gate and the shooting ceased.

Indeed, there was to be a celebration at the Castle; the guests were received with flags and a salute. Several military men sat in the carriages; perhaps Otto, the lieutenant, was among them.

Johannes descended from the mound and set off for home. He was overtaken by a man from the Castle, who stopped him. The man carried a letter in his cap; he had been sent by Miss Victoria and was to have an answer.

Johannes read the letter with a pounding heart. Victoria invited him after all, wrote to him in heartfelt words, and asked him to come. This time she would ask him. Reply by the messenger.

A strange and unexpected joy had befallen him; the blood rose to his head, and he answered the man that he would come—yes, thank you, he would come at once.

There you are!

He handed the messenger a ridiculously large coin and hurried home to dress.

VIII

For the first time in his life, he passed through the Castle gate and went up the stairs to the second floor. The murmur of voices came toward him from within; his heart beat hard; he knocked and entered.

The still-young lady of the Castle came toward him and greeted him kindly, pressing his hand. She was pleased to see him; she remembered him from the time when he had been no taller than this; now he was a great man .... And it was as though the lady of the Castle had meant to say something more; she held his hand for a long time and looked at him searchingly.

The lord of the Castle also came forward and offered him his hand. As his wife had said, a great man, in more than one sense. A famous man. He was very pleased ...

He was introduced to gentlemen and ladies, to the chamberlain, who wore his decorations, to the chamberlain’s wife, to a landowner from the neighboring district, to Otto, the lieutenant. He did not see Victoria.

A considerable time passed. Victoria entered, pale, even uncertain; she was leading a young girl by the hand. They made a circuit of the drawing room, greeted everyone, and spoke a little with each person. They stopped beside Johannes.

9—Hamsun: III
Victoria smiled and said:

Look, here is Camilla; is that not a surprise? You know each other.

She stood for a little while and looked at them both, then left the drawing room.

For the first moment Johannes remained standing rigid and bewildered on the spot. Here was the surprise; Victoria had most kindly provided someone else in her place. Listen here, go now and have each other, you people! Spring is in bloom, the sun is shining; throw open the windows if you wish, for there is fragrance in the garden, and starlings are also playing in the tops of the birches out there. Why do you not speak to each other? But then laugh now!
